places.name: Earth
places.blurb: Strong gravity. Hot air rises fast.

labMaterials.name: Paper
labMaterials.fact: Paper is made of wood fibers, so it catches fire very easily.

labMaterials.name: Cotton shirt
labMaterials.fact: Cotton comes from a plant. It burns easily, so astronauts wear special fabrics.

labMaterials.name: Plastic (acrylic)
labMaterials.fact: Astronauts burned acrylic on the space station in the BASS experiment to watch flames spread.

labMaterials.name: Fire-safe fabric
labMaterials.fact: Nomex is used in firefighter and astronaut suits. In normal air it puts itself out!

labMaterials.name: Teflon
labMaterials.fact: Teflon almost never burns, even with lots of extra oxygen.

labMaterials.name: Fuel droplet
labMaterials.fact: NASA's FLEX experiment burned tiny fuel drops held on a thin thread to study space flames.

lessons.title: Fire needs three friends
lessons.text: Every fire needs FUEL (something to burn), HEAT (a spark) and OXYGEN (from the air). Find all three labels in the lab. The little blue pairs are oxygen molecules!

lessons.title: Hot air rises
lessons.text: Watch the grey smoke float straight up and set off the smoke alarm on the ceiling. Gravity lets hot, light air rise, and that pulls the flame into a teardrop.

lessons.title: Fire in space
lessons.text: Now we are on the space station. Nothing is "up" anymore, so the flame turns into a blue ball and the smoke spreads slowly. Does the smoke alarm beep this time?

lessons.title: Moon base: extra oxygen
lessons.text: On Earth, fire-safe fabric puts itself out. A Moon base may have 34% oxygen, and now it burns! This is why NASA tests materials in the real air astronauts will breathe.

lessons.title: Sneaky invisible flames
lessons.text: Let us put out this space fire with the red extinguisher. Watch closely… then switch on Heat vision. Is it really out?

lessons.title: Your turn, fire scientist!
lessons.text: Try Mars with plastic, or lower the oxygen until the fire goes out by itself. Can you find the material that never burns?
